problem.title: Three things that don’t work — and nobody fixes them

items.title: Homes that aren’t real
items.body: Below-market price, perfect photos, hot area. You call and nobody answers — or someone answers who wants to sell you a lead list. Portals react to reports because they live on listing volume.

items.title: Commission on both sides
items.body: 3% plus VAT from the seller and 3% plus VAT from the buyer, on the same home. On €300,000 that is nearly €22,000 leaving the deal.

items.title: Nobody knows who can buy
items.body: Sellers don’t know if a visitor will get a mortgage. Visitors often don’t know either. Months are lost finding out.

steps.title: Every listing has a verified owner
steps.body: Identity confirmed and title checked before publication. If a listing stops getting answers, it leaves the platform. Publishing here is free, so verification costs us nothing — portals sell the inventory they refuse to clean.

steps.title: Values are the official ones
steps.body: Every property shows the market band recorded by the Agenzia delle Entrate for its micro-zone, next to the asking price. If the price is off-band, we say so — and we say to ask why.

steps.title: Buying capacity is verified; the name is not
steps.body: Sellers see that a buyer can sustain the purchase, with an indicative range and an expiry. They don’t see the surname and don’t get the phone number. Details are exchanged only when both sides confirm the viewing at the same time.

steps.title: No commission from the seller
steps.body: We earn from the services you choose — photos, energy certificate, document checks — at a fixed price stated before you order. The same on a €150,000 home and an €800,000 one.

sellers.title: The highest estimate isn’t a compliment
sellers.body: Anyone who only earns if you sign a mandate has a reason to promise a price the market won’t pay. Then, after three months without viewings, comes the call about cutting the price. We take no commission on the sale. We have no reason to inflate the number.

buyers.title: Do you already know what you can spend?
buyers.body: Searching, contacting and booking viewings is free and stays free. Before you fall for a home, you can have your buying capacity checked for free — and show up as someone who can buy, not as one of twenty who called today.

languages.title: In Italian, English and Spanish
languages.body: Not only the interface. Every document you sign comes with an explanation in a language you actually read: what a proposal commits you to, why the notary is not your lawyer, what happens if you change your mind.

transparency.title: Who pays us — and who doesn’t

hero.title: Buy in Italy
hero.standfirst: The property is the easy part. What stops foreign buyers is a paper trail in a language they don't read, signed in front of people whose job they misunderstand. We run that part for you, start to keys.

trapsSection.title: Four things nobody tells you until it's too late
trapsSection.lede: These aren't edge cases. They're the standard ways a purchase from abroad turns into a loss, and each one is preventable in the week before you sign.

traps.title: Your offer is a contract
traps.body: Once the seller accepts, you are bound. There is no cooling-off period. Buyers routinely sign this believing it's an expression of interest.

traps.title: The notary isn't your lawyer
traps.body: A notaio is a neutral public official who certifies the deed. They do not negotiate for you, and they are not obliged to tell you a price is bad.

traps.title: The floor plan must match the building
traps.body: If the registered plan doesn't match what's actually built, the deed can be challenged and mortgage lending refused. Unpermitted verandas are everywhere.

traps.title: Deposits are not all the same
traps.body: A caparra and an acconto look identical on a bank transfer and behave completely differently if the deal collapses. Only one gets you double back.

path.title: Every step, who does it, how long it takes
path.lede: This is the actual sequence of an Italian purchase. Steps marked in gold are where money is most often lost.

steps.what: Your Italian tax identity. Nothing — no offer, no bank account, no utility contract — happens without it. We obtain it through the consulate or Agenzia delle Entrate.
We pull the ownership chain, mortgages, liens and seizures registered against the property, plus the cadastral plan. Done before you offer, not after.
Drafted with the conditions that protect you — mortgage clause, conformity clause, deadline. Binding on acceptance, so the wording is the whole game.
The real contract. We register it at the Agenzia delle Entrate and, where your deposit warrants it, transcribe it at the Conservatoria so no one can sell the property twice.
Required to issue the assegni circolari used at completion. Opening one as a non-resident is slower than you expect; we start it in parallel at step 01.
Signed before the notaio. If you can't attend, we arrange a procura speciale so someone signs on your behalf — legalised and apostilled in your country first.
Cadastral transfer, electricity, gas, water, waste tax and the condominium register moved into your name. The unglamorous part where foreign owners get stuck for months.

tiersSection.title: Fixed fees. Agreed before we start.
tiersSection.lede: Third-party costs — notary, taxes, cadastral fees, translations — are passed through at cost with the receipt attached. We don't mark them up.

commission.title: What a €300,000 purchase actually costs you
commission.lede: Italian agencies conventionally charge a percentage to both sides of the same transaction. We charge the buyer a fixed fee and take nothing from the seller, so nobody on our side is paid more when you pay more.
commission.srcBody: No Italian law sets a minimum commission — the Antitrust authority confirmed in 2004 that tariffs do not apply to this sector, and art. 6 of L. 39/1989 leaves the rate to agreement between the parties. The 3% figure is the customary rate recorded in Chamber of Commerce usage tables, which apply only where the parties agreed nothing in writing. That is the trap: an unsigned or silent mandate can be back-filled at the local customary rate. Ours states the fee before work starts.

compare.sub: 3% + IVA. The seller is customarily charged the same again on the same sale.
Fixed fee incl. IVA. Identical on a €300,000 flat or a €900,000 villa.

compare.lbl: Paid to us by the seller
compare.sub: Always. It's the reason we can tell you to walk away from a property.

faq.q: Can I buy in Italy if I'm not an EU citizen?
faq.a: Usually yes, but it depends on your nationality. Italy applies a reciprocity condition — you can buy if an Italian could buy in your country, or if a treaty covers it. Buyers from the UK, US, Canada, Australia, Switzerland and most of Latin America are covered. We confirm your position in writing before you pay anything.

faq.q: Do I have to be in Italy to complete?
faq.a: No. You can grant a procura speciale — a specific power of attorney — allowing someone to sign the deed for you. It has to be executed in front of a notary in your country and then legalised or apostilled, which takes two to three weeks. We start that early so it never becomes the reason completion slips.

No. We're paid a fixed fee by you and nothing by the seller, which means we have no stake in whether a particular property sells. If the survey comes back badly, our advice is to walk, and it costs us nothing to say so.

Notary fees, registration and cadastral taxes, translation and apostille costs, and any technical survey by a geometra. These are passed through at cost with the invoice attached. On a €300,000 second home, budget roughly €9,000–13,000 in taxes and notary fees depending on the region and whether you buy from a private seller or a company.

faq.q: An agent told me 3% is fixed by law. Is it?
faq.a: No. There is no legal minimum commission in Italy. Rates are freely negotiable and have been since the sector was liberalised. The 3% you'll hear quoted is the customary figure recorded by local Chambers of Commerce, and it applies as a fallback only when the parties never agreed anything in writing — which is exactly why you should never sign a mandate that leaves the rate blank.

faq.q: Which languages do you work in?
faq.a: Italian, English and Spanish, with every document you sign accompanied by a plain translation. We won't put a contract in front of you that you can only read in Italian.

compare.kicker: Why the numbers never add up
compare.title: The highest estimate isn’t a compliment.
compare.lede: In Italy the easiest way to win a mandate is to promise a price the market won’t pay. Then, after months with no viewings, comes the call to cut the price.

usual.title: A number built to convince you
usual.body: Three agencies, three different figures, none that explain where they came from. Whoever values you only earns if you sign — so the estimate is there to get the signature, not to help you sell.

here.title: A number you can check
here.body: We start from the values the Agenzia delle Entrate records for your microzone, and we show every part of the calculation. We take no seller commission, so we have no reason to inflate it.

method.title: We show the sums, not only the total.
method.lede: Every valuation shows what it rests on. Where a figure is estimated rather than recorded, we say so.

factors.body: The value band the Agenzia delle Entrate records for the property’s specific zone — not the whole municipality. In Milan the gap between two zones can exceed 300%.
OMI values are per m² of gross area. Using net floor area skews the result by 15–25%: we convert before calculating and tell you which base we used.
The Agency publishes distinct bands for average, excellent and poor condition. We use the right band instead of an eyeballed percentage.
Floor, lift, outlook, terrace, garage. Every adjustment is listed with its weight, so you can challenge it if you disagree.

next.title: The number is yours. Even if you do nothing else.
next.lede: Keep it — to decide, to challenge someone else’s figure, or to wait. If you want to sell, you publish here with no commission.

optionA.title: Take the number and go
optionA.body: No follow-up, no call, no newsletter. If you come back in six months the valuation updates with new data.

optionB.title: List with no commission
optionB.body: Your listing, your contacts, your viewings. Add-ons you choose — photos, documents, EPC — have a fixed price shown before you order.

items.q: If it’s free, how do you make money?
items.a: From services you choose, not from the sale. Photography, energy certificate, document checks, deal support: each has a fixed price shown before you order, the same on a €150,000 home and an €800,000 one. We take no seller commission.
No. We don’t pass your address or details to agencies, and there is no agent network buying these leads. If you want to talk to someone, you ask.

It’s an estimate, and we treat it as one: we give a range, not a single figure. OMI values are official but by definition approximate — they describe the microzone band, not your exact flat. A surveyor’s appraisal is different, and we say so instead of pretending an algorithm is enough.

items.q: Where does the data come from?
items.a: From the Agenzia delle Entrate’s Osservatorio del Mercato Immobiliare, which publishes recorded values every six months for every microzone in every Italian municipality. Banks and valuers use the same reference. We always cite the semester.
Yes. Coverage is national: 7,866 municipalities, every province.

mediationPage.metaDescription: No Italian law sets a minimum mediation fee. What the rules actually say, where the 3% comes from, and what to check before you sign a mandate.
mediationPage.sub: If someone told you the minimum commission is fixed by law, they told you something false. Here is what the rules actually say.
mediationPage.stamp: Information page · not a substitute for legal advice

law.title: What the law says
law.p1: Estate mediation is governed by Law 39 of 1989. On the amount of the commission, Article 6 says only one thing: it is set by the parties.
law.p2: There is no minimum tariff. There has never been a binding tariff for this sector, and in 2004 the Italian Competition Authority expressly confirmed that tariffs do not apply. The amount is freely negotiated.
lines: L. 39/1989, art. 6 — the commission is set by the parties
AGCM, decision no. 13035/2004 — tariffs not applicable to the sector
Art. 1755 Italian Civil Code — the right accrues when the deal concludes

origin.title: So where does the 3% come from?
origin.p1: From the collections of commercial customs kept by Chambers of Commerce. Each chamber records customary percentages for its province — often around 3% from each of the two parties, plus VAT.
origin.p2After: , not statutes. They fill a gap: they apply only when the parties have not agreed anything in writing. If an amount is agreed, that amount prevails.
origin.p3: Courts, for that matter, have gone well below that threshold when the work done did not justify it: in a case decided by the Venice Tribunal, 0.5% of the property value was held reasonable because the agent had neither conducted the negotiation nor collected the offer.

paras: Silence does not work in your favour. A mandate that does not state the commission can be referred back to local customs — that is, in many provinces, exactly that 3% from both parties.
Never sign a mandate with a blank percentage, "to be agreed", or deferred to an annex you have not read.

when.title: When the commission is due
when.p1Before: Not on signing the mandate, and not when a potential buyer appears. The right accrues on
when.p1After: : when the parties are bound, typically on an accepted offer.
when.p2: Until then, any figure you are shown is an estimate, not a debt. If a quote does not say so, ask for it in writing.

asteGuida.title: The Italian Property Auction Guide — 10 essential checks before you bid
asteGuida.intro: Italian judicial auctions follow precise rules. Successful buyers aren’t luckier — they check the right things in the right order. This guide lists the 10 essential checks, written also for those who didn’t grow up inside the Italian system.
asteGuida.printHint: Tip: use your browser’s Print dialog to save a PDF.

checks.title: Where to find auctions
checks.body: Start with pvp.giustizia.it — the official public sales portal (Portale delle Vendite Pubbliche). Tribunal-specific sale portals are also worth checking. Consulting them is free. Focus on areas you already know: local knowledge reduces surprises on price, logistics, and resale.

checks.title: The court expert’s report
checks.body: The perizia written by the CTU (consulente tecnico d’ufficio — the court-appointed technical expert) is the core document. Read all of it, not just the first page. It covers condition, provenance, building and cadastral irregularities, and often occupancy and costs. It is long and written in legal Italian — which is exactly where valuation mistakes start.

checks.title: Occupancy
checks.body: Vacant (libero), occupied by the debtor, or occupied by a tenant with an opposable lease: three different purchases. Time-to-possession is a real cost (temporary housing, delayed works, yield). Check what the perizia and sale notice say, and what remains to be cleared after you win.

checks.title: Building & cadastral irregularities
checks.body: Check difformità and abusi: whether they can be regularised (sanabilità) and at what cost. They affect mortgage eligibility, insurance, and resale. A fixable issue is not free — budget it before you raise your bid.

checks.title: Mortgages & seizures
checks.body: As a rule, registered mortgages (ipoteche) and seizures (pignoramenti) are cancelled by the transfer decree (decreto di trasferimento) — you do not inherit them as in an ordinary sale. Check the perizia for exceptions. Do not assume: read the relevant section and get help if unclear.

checks.title: Condominium arrears
checks.body: The buyer can owe condominium fees for the current year and the previous year (art. 63 disp. att. c.c.). Ask the sale organiser for the administrator’s statement with the figure. It is not a detail — it can move the real cost by thousands of euros.

checks.title: True total cost
checks.body: The hammer price (aggiudicazione) is not the total. Add taxes, cancellation fees, technical/notary costs, renovation, and waiting time. Set your maximum before the auction and never exceed it — bidding emotion is the fastest way to erase your margin.

checks.title: What you need to bid
checks.body: You need a codice fiscale (Italian tax code), ID documents, and usually a cauzione (deposit — often 10% of the starting price). For telematic auctions you also need a PEC email (certified email) and a firma digitale (digital signature). Non-residents can obtain all of these — plan 2–4 weeks ahead. Without them ready, your bid cannot proceed.

checks.title: Auction day
checks.body: Know the minimum offer versus the starting price (prezzo base), the minimum raise (rilancio minimo), and the deadlines. Deadlines are strict (perentori): a formal defect excludes the bid. Arrive with documents already checked; do not improvise in the room or on the platform.

checks.title: After winning
checks.body: Pay the balance (saldo prezzo) within the term — missing it forfeits the deposit. Then comes the decreto di trasferimento and voltura (ownership update). If you need financing, it must follow the court’s timeline, not the bank’s: align the loan before you bid.
